title: Arrays in .data
description: Contiguous bytes and indexed addressing modes
theory:
### Contiguous bytes, words, and quadwords

An **array** in assembly is mostly an address plus a stride. You define storage with
**`db`**, **`dw`**, **`dd`**, or **`dq`** and refer to elements with indexed addressing
modes such as **`byte [array + rcx]`** or **`qword [array + rcx*8]`**.

The **`equ`** pseudo-op is handy for sizes (`len equ $ - msg`) but remember **`$`**
evaluates at assembly time, so it captures the distance from the label’s base address
at the point where it appears in the source.

### Indexing and bounds

Hardware does not check array bounds: an out-of-range index silently reads or clobbers
adjacent memory. In learning exercises you compute indices carefully; in production you
prove them safe in a higher layer or insert explicit checks.

```nasm
section .data
    scores: db 10, 20, 30

section .text
; rcx = logical index 0..2
    movzx eax, byte [rel scores + rcx]
```

### Alignment and performance

Natural alignment (`dd` on 4-byte boundaries, `dq` on 8-byte boundaries) avoids split
access penalties on some cores. NASM lays out items sequentially; insert explicit **`align`**
directives when you care about cache-line or SIMD alignment even in userspace samples.

exercises.title: First element
exercises.description: `.data` holds `db 'A','B','C'`. Print only the first byte (`A`, no newline), then exit 0.
exercises.starter_code:
global _start
section .data
    arr: db 'A','B','C'
section .text
_start:
    ; write 1 byte from arr
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
exercises.solution:
global _start
section .data
    arr: db 'A', 'B', 'C'
section .text
_start:
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    lea rsi, [rel arr]
    mov rdx, 1
    syscall
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall

exercises.title: Walk indices
exercises.description: Sum the three **numeric** bytes `2`, `3`, `4` stored in `.data` into an 8-bit register (result `9`). Print one character digit `9` (no newline), then exit 0.
exercises.starter_code:
global _start
section .data
    nums: db 2, 3, 4
section .text
_start:
    xor al, al
    ; add nums[0..2] into al (watch zero-extension)
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
hints: Clear a register, add bytes with `movzx` into a wider reg, sum, then add `'0'` only if result <10
exercises.solution:
global _start
section .data
    nums: db 2, 3, 4
section .text
_start:
    xor ecx, ecx
    movzx eax, byte [rel nums]
    add ecx, eax
    movzx eax, byte [rel nums+1]
    add ecx, eax
    movzx eax, byte [rel nums+2]
    add ecx, eax
    add ecx, '0'
    mov [rel digit], cl
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    lea rsi, [rel digit]
    mov rdx, 1
    syscall
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
section .bss
    digit: resb 1

exercises.title: Whole buffer write
exercises.description: Print the three-byte buffer `db 'x','y','z'` with a **single** `write` syscall (no newline), then exit 0.
exercises.starter_code:
global _start
section .data
    buf: db 'x','y','z'
    blen equ $ - buf
section .text
_start:
    ; one syscall rdx=blen
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
exercises.solution:
global _start
section .data
    buf: db 'x', 'y', 'z'
    blen equ $ - buf
section .text
_start:
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    lea rsi, [rel buf]
    mov rdx, blen
    syscall
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall

exercises.title: Last element
exercises.description: Same buffer `db 'A','B','C'`. Print only the **last** byte (`C`, no newline) using `lea` with offset `2`, then exit 0.
exercises.starter_code:
global _start
section .data
    arr: db 'A','B','C'
section .text
_start:
    ; rsi -> arr+2, rdx=1, write
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
exercises.solution:
global _start
section .data
    arr: db 'A', 'B', 'C'
section .text
_start:
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    lea rsi, [rel arr+2]
    mov rdx, 1
    syscall
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
